Approach Cherbourg-en-Cotentin via small towns and bays, with moderate local traffic. The riding is not highly technical but varied enough to stay interesting.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Ride east along Normandy’s northern coast via secondary roads and occasional short N-road links, avoiding prolonged autoroute use. The route includes chalk cliffs, river crossings, and rolling farmland.

Traffic can be heavier near Le Havre and other larger towns, but the road surfaces are generally good and cornering is moderate. It’s a longer day but realistic with regular fuel and rest opportunities.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Continue northeast from Dieppe along the Channel coast, using D-roads parallel to the main corridors. The riding features low cliffs, dunes, and industrial ports, with a mix of straights and soft curves.

Cross into Belgium near the Dunkerque–Nieuwpoort stretch and finish in Ostend, following Belgian coastal roads. Pavement is good, but expect more traffic and urban sections near resort towns, concluding a practical, scenic cross-border coastal run.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Bolzano on the SS241 towards Nova Levante, climbing steadily into the Dolomites on a beautifully paved mountain road. The route quickly turns into a series of linked curves and elevation changes, with good asphalt but frequent tight bends that demand smooth throttle and careful corner entry.

Continue toward Canazei via Passo Costalunga and the Val di Fassa, staying on scenic, secondary mountain roads. Traffic can include buses and other motorcyclists, especially in summer, and some sections are narrow with limited guardrails, so maintain a controlled pace and enjoy the dramatic rock formations.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
From Canazei, attack the famous Passo Pordoi with its stacked hairpins and strong elevation gain. The surface is good but the corners are tight and frequent, ideal for experienced riders who enjoy technical switchback work.

Drop to Arabba and continue the classic Sellaronda direction toward Corvara, riding a loop of high passes and balcony roads. Expect exposed sections, quick changes in weather, and heavy tourist traffic at times, but the riding is some of the best in Europe, combining precise cornering with unforgettable scenery.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Climb over Passo Gardena, another Dolomite classic with a mix of hairpins, medium-radius bends, and panoramic views. The asphalt is mostly excellent, but early mornings can bring moisture and gravel at the apexes, so choose lines carefully.

Descend toward Ortisei and then head north toward Vipiteno via smaller valley roads and, where possible, avoiding long motorway stretches. The route alternates between tight mountain segments and flowing valley sections, giving a balanced day of technical and relaxed riding.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
From Vipiteno, climb the Jaufenpass on a narrower, very twisty mountain road with numerous hairpins and strong elevation change. This pass demands focus: corners can be blind, and some sections are exposed without much room for error.

Descend toward Merano and return to Bolzano on a mix of curving valley roads and well-surfaced secondary routes. The final leg is less technical but still scenic, passing vineyards and orchards, a satisfying way to complete a concentrated Dolomite switchback tour.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Florence on SP and SR backroads into the Chianti hills, avoiding the main Autostrada. The roads immediately become more interesting, with rolling curves, varied elevation, and smooth asphalt threading through vineyards and olive groves.

The run to Greve and Radda in Chianti is a classic combination of medium-speed sweepers and short technical sections in villages. Expect occasional tight, blind bends and narrow stone-lined roads, ideal for an agile bike and riders who enjoy reading the terrain.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Head through Gaiole on minor Chianti roads, a patchwork of twisting lanes and short straights that reward smooth, flowing riding. Surfaces are generally good but can include patched sections and occasional gravel near field entrances.

Approach Siena via scenic SR roads, passing hilltop villages and cypress-lined lanes. The final kilometers into Siena bring busier traffic and some cobbled surfaces in the historic area, so it is wise to slow down and manage heat and clutch use carefully.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Ride southeast from Siena toward Asciano via the Crete Senesi, with undulating, open roads and wide views over rolling clay hills. Curves are more flowing than tight, making this a day for stable mid-speed cornering and enjoying the scenery.

Continue to Montalcino on narrower hill roads with more frequent bends and tighter village entries. The pavement is generally good, but watch for broken edges and occasional livestock-related debris in rural stretches.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Spend a shorter day threading iconic Val d’Orcia roads, where every hillside seems designed for postcards and motorcycle photography. The routes between Montalcino, San Quirico, and Montepulciano blend smooth asphalt with gently tightening bends.

Traffic is usually modest, but summer can bring tourist convoys and cyclists. Visibility is good, and elevation changes are moderate, making this a relaxed but engaging day of classic Tuscan riding.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Roll north toward Cortona and Arezzo on SR roads that mix gentle curves with occasional short, tighter sections. The terrain becomes slightly more wooded, and pavements remain generally good, with some traffic near larger towns.

Return to Florence using secondary highways rather than the Autostrada, completing a full Chianti and Val d’Orcia loop. The final stretch is less technical but still pleasant, ideal for cooling down from several days of hill riding.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Naples on the Sorrentina peninsula, avoiding major motorways and using coastal and hill roads that can be busy but rewarding. Expect tight village traffic, many roundabouts, and occasional rough patches, but overall decent asphalt.

The run from Sorrento to Positano on the SS163 is legendary: carved into cliffs with tight corners, sheer drops, and continuous scenery. Traffic is heavy and often slow, so this section is about precise low-speed control and enjoying the views rather than high pace.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Continue along the Amalfi Coast, threading the SS163’s continuous bends and compressed traffic. The road is narrow, often with buses and parked vehicles encroaching into your lane, so lane positioning and patience are critical.

From Amalfi, ride east to Salerno, where the coast gradually opens and the road relaxes slightly. Pavement is generally good, but frequent speed limits and traffic controls make this a technical but lower-speed day.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Head south along the Cilento coast on secondary roads with fewer tourists than Amalfi. Curves are steady, elevation is moderate, and the mix of coastal and inland lanes provides an excellent riding rhythm.

Approaching Agropoli and Santa Maria di Castellabate, expect some narrow urban sections and variable surface quality, but nothing extreme. This is a rewarding, more relaxed coastal day with plenty of places to pause near the sea.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Ride further south through the Cilento and into the rugged coast around Palinuro and Maratea. Roads here are curvier and more varied, with significant elevation changes and frequent blind bends as they wrap around cliffs and hills.

Pavement is generally decent but can have broken edges and occasional gravel washed onto the road after rain. Traffic is lighter than around Amalfi, making this an excellent day for more spirited but still careful riding.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
From Maratea, ride a mix of coastal and inland roads toward Sapri, then climb toward Potenza. The inland mountain roads give a different flavor: tighter, more rural, with occasional rough surfaces and fewer services.

This final day demands more attention to fuel and weather, but offers satisfying cornering and changing scenery. Ending in Potenza positions you well for onward travel while closing a varied coastal-and-mountain loop.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Bologna heading southwest onto the smaller mountain roads of the northern Apennines. The climb toward Porretta Terme offers a series of medium-radius bends, consistent elevation gain, and generally good asphalt, though some sections can narrow suddenly.

Cross into Tuscany near Pistoia on secondary passes with more hairpins and tighter sequences of corners. Traffic is light compared to the plains, but visibility can be limited in forested sections, especially under mixed weather.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Ride up toward San Marcello Piteglio and Abetone, climbing into higher Apennine territory on classic Italian mountain roads. Expect numerous switchbacks, steep gradients, and some sections with variable surface quality due to winter damage.

Descend north-west toward Castelnovo ne’ Monti on less-traveled mountain routes, where traffic is minimal and cornering is continuous. The day is physically demanding but extremely rewarding for riders comfortable with sustained twisties.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
From Castelnovo ne’ Monti, cross Passo del Cerreto, a rugged, scenic pass with many bends and changing pavement quality. Some sections are narrow and exposed, so corner speeds must be chosen conservatively.

Drop toward Aulla and La Spezia, where roads gradually widen and traffic increases. The final stretch combines mountain descents with views of the Ligurian coast, easing you from high passes to sea-level riding.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Head inland through the Lunigiana area toward Pontremoli on smaller, curving roads that climb back into the Apennine spine. These routes are less busy but can have rough patches and tight village corners.

Continue to Parma via minor passes and valley roads, avoiding the main Autostrada. The day offers a nice mix of twisties and more relaxed valley sections, closing a satisfying north–south Apennine rollercoaster.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Start in Olbia and ride inland toward Nuoro on Sardinia’s famously smooth, curvy roads. The SS routes here are designed with sweeping bends, moderate gradients, and good sightlines, making them exceptionally enjoyable for motorcycles.

Continue to Orgosolo via smaller mountain roads that tighten and become more technical, with occasional rough surfaces and narrower widths. Traffic is light, but livestock and local vehicles can appear unexpectedly, so keep speeds controlled.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Ride further into the central Sardinian highlands, visiting villages like Fonni and Aritzo on winding mountain roads. Elevation is higher here, with switchbacks, undulating ridgelines, and varied pavement quality, from near-perfect to patched.

This day is heavily focused on cornering and elevation changes rather than distance, ideal for riders who enjoy sustained technical riding with minimal traffic and big views.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Continue through the interior villages on twisty, narrower roads, then gradually head west toward Bosa. As you get closer to the coast, the terrain softens and the roads open, but they still offer frequent bends and strong riding character.

Approaching Bosa, choose the coastal SP roads where possible, which combine smooth surfaces with sweeping seaside curves. This transition from interior mountains to the western shore makes for a varied, satisfying day.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Ride the Bosa–Alghero coastal road, one of Sardinia’s best known motorcycle stretches, featuring continuous curves, cliffs, and excellent asphalt. It is not highly technical but extremely engaging, with changing radii and open views over the sea.

From Alghero back to Olbia, follow inland and coastal secondary routes that maintain a good mix of bends and straights. Traffic can increase near towns, but the overall riding remains enjoyable and appropriate for a final day.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Milan on smaller roads toward Lecco, avoiding highway-heavy sections where possible. The ride around the eastern side of Lake Como immediately introduces lakeside curves and moderate traffic, demanding smooth lane positioning.

Continue to Sondrio along the Valtellina valley, where the road follows the river with flowing bends and good pavement. It is more a valley cruise than a tight mountain pass, offering a pleasant warm-up before heading toward higher alpine terrain.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Ride up-valley to Tirano, then cross into Switzerland and climb toward the Bernina Pass. The ascent features a mix of broad curves and tighter switchbacks, with well-maintained alpine asphalt and strong elevation changes.

Descending toward St. Moritz, the road remains high-quality but can be busy with tourist traffic and buses. This is high mountain riding with exposure, rapid weather shifts, and some sections where guardrails are minimal, rewarding careful pace control.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Head south via the Maloja Pass toward Chiavenna, tackling a series of tight hairpins and steep gradients. The surface is excellent but the corners are stacked, demanding attention and good low-gear control.

From Chiavenna, ride down toward Lake Como on valley roads and then along the lakeside toward Como. Traffic increases and the roads narrow along the lake, but the combination of views and curves remains very appealing for touring bikes.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Finish the loop via secondary roads through Varese, avoiding prolonged Autostrada segments. The terrain is rolling, with gentle bends and frequent towns, giving a relaxed feel after the high mountain passes.

Return to Milan with a short, practical final leg, navigating busier suburban traffic. This day is less about technical riding and more about wrapping up a coherent cross-border alpine tour.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Depart the Venice/Mestre area on secondary roads toward Treviso and Udine, passing through flat plains and agricultural zones. The roads are mostly straight with gentle curves, well paved and with moderate traffic, suitable for relaxed touring.

Approaching Udine, avoid the main Autostrada and follow regional highways that maintain a good flow without high speeds. This day sets up the approach to the alpine foothills and the Slovenian border.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Ride east to Cividale del Friuli on minor roads, then approach the Slovenian border near Kobarid using scenic, curvier routes along river valleys. The crossing is straightforward, and the roads immediately gain riding character with more bends and elevation changes.

From Kobarid to Tolmin, follow the Soča Valley, a favorite among motorcyclists for its combination of turquoise river, narrow gorge segments, and twisting asphalt. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel on the edges and occasional tour buses.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Continue southeast through Slovenian backroads toward Idrija and Postojna, riding on narrower, more technical roads. These routes feature frequent bends, moderate elevation changes, and mixed forest and rural scenery, ideal for agile mid-size motorcycles.

The pavement is mostly good but can show patchwork repairs; blind corners in wooded sections require disciplined speeds. Arriving in Postojna gives access to services and a natural pause point after a day of engaged riding.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Ride toward the Adriatic coast via Trieste, mixing inland curves with coastal cliffside roads. Traffic picks up closer to the city, with tighter urban junctions and more complex navigation, but the views over the Gulf of Trieste are rewarding.

Head northwest to Monfalcone on coastal and plains roads, mostly broader and less technical. This is a calmer, transitional day as you move back toward Italy’s flat northeast.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Complete the loop via Palmanova and back to Mestre on regional roads. The landscape is largely flat, with long straights and gentle curves, and the pavement is good, making this a simple, low-stress final leg.

Near Venice/Mestre, traffic becomes busy with local and tourist flows, so heightened awareness is important despite the simple road geometry. The day neatly closes a cross-border Adriatic and Soča Valley tour.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Turin on backroads toward Biella, riding through Piedmont hills on a mix of gentle bends and small town entries. Pavement is mostly good, with some patched sections on lesser-used lanes.

Continue to Arona on Lake Maggiore’s western shore, where traffic increases but the lakeside views compensate. Curves are smoother rather than tight, and the day serves as a scenic warm-up for the alpine sections ahead.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Ride north along Lake Maggiore toward Stresa, then turn into the Ossola valley toward Domodossola. The roads here mix lakeside traffic with increasingly mountainous terrain and more frequent curves.

Cross into Switzerland through the Simplon Pass corridor toward Brig-Glis. The ascent and descent feature wide, well-engineered alpine roads, tunnels, and long-radius bends, excellent for loaded touring bikes, though weather and altitude require attention.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Head up the upper Rhone valley toward Gletsch and then Andermatt, entering the heart of Swiss pass country. This segment can include famous passes such as Furka or Grimsel depending on the exact route, with stacked hairpins, strong elevation, and excellent but demanding pavement.

Traffic includes many bikes and sports cars, and weather can change quickly at altitude. This is high-intensity riding that rewards precise braking, cornering, and situational awareness.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Ride over or around the Gotthard area, using the old pass road where conditions allow for a more historic, twisty experience, or the newer route for smoother travel. Cobblestones and tight bends on the old road demand extra care.

Descend toward Bellinzona on valley roads with good surfaces and a mix of tunnels and open stretches. The route becomes less technical but remains scenic, transitioning from high alpine to southern, more Mediterranean-feeling terrain.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Follow the lakes and valleys south through Lugano and back into Italy near Como, riding a combination of lakeside and inland roads. Traffic is heavier but the scenery and smooth asphalt keep the ride enjoyable.

Return to Milan on regional roads, avoiding long Autostrada stints. The final day is less about passes and more about comfortable, scenic transit back to the city.

title: Istrian Detour via Slovenia and Croatia
subtitle: A 5-day tour of Italy

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Trieste on coastal roads and cross into Slovenia near Koper, using local border crossings suited to motorcycles. The roads are well paved, with a blend of gentle curves and short urban sections.

Continue to Piran on the Slovenian coast via narrower seaside roads and short hillside bends. Traffic is moderate and surfaces generally good, but village sections can be tight and busy.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Ride south into Croatia’s Istria peninsula, crossing the border near Umag. The coastal roads here feature moderate curves, varied elevation, and usually good asphalt, with occasional heavy holiday traffic.

Continue to Poreč on a mix of coastal and slightly inland routes, with more relaxed riding than mountain passes but still plenty of cornering. Watch for local speed enforcement and variable surfaces near older villages.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Follow the western Istrian coast south, riding secondary roads that weave between farmland and shoreline. Curves are gentle, and the pavement is generally decent, though some stretches can be patched and uneven.

Rovinj and Pula are both busy coastal towns with more urban riding, including cobbles and tight streets. This is a lower-speed, more atmospheric day focused on coastal touring rather than technical riding.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Head northeast across Istria toward Labin and Opatija, using hillier inland roads with more curves and elevation changes. The scenery shifts from flat coastal to hillside viewpoints, with asphalt that ranges from good to moderately worn.

Approaching Opatija, the road drops back toward the Kvarner Gulf coastline, with sweeping bends and stronger riding character. Traffic can be heavier near seaside resorts, but the route remains engaging.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Ride through Rijeka and back toward the Slovenian border, then return to Trieste on a combination of coastal and inland highways. The roads are wider and less technical but still feature enough bends to interest motorcyclists.

Border crossings are straightforward, and traffic volumes are higher near cities, so the emphasis is on safe, smooth progress. This final day closes a realistic multi-country Istrian loop that starts and ends in Italy.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Start in Bari and ride southeast along the Adriatic coast toward Brindisi, using SS and coastal SP roads that favor gentle curves and good views over the sea. Pavement is generally good, with some busy sections near industrial areas.

Continue to Lecce on inland routes through olive groves and low hills. The roads here are simpler but pleasant, with moderate traffic and frequent small roundabouts that keep you attentive.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Ride the eastern Salento coast from Lecce to Otranto and then down to Santa Maria di Leuca. The coastline here provides an enjoyable mix of sweeping curves, short climbs and descents, and varied pavement quality that is generally decent.

Traffic is lighter than around Bari, though summer brings tourists and campers. The route remains ideal for a mid-speed touring pace, with frequent options to stop at viewpoints or small seaside towns.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Turn up the western side of Salento, riding a mix of coastal and inland roads toward Gallipoli and Taranto. The terrain is flat to gently rolling, and curves are moderate, making this a comfortable day focused on local scenery and easy handling.

Approaching Taranto, expect more industrial areas and heavier traffic, with roundabouts and junctions requiring careful lane discipline. Pavement remains mostly good but can be less uniform in older sections.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Ride inland toward Matera on hilly routes that introduce more elevation and bends. The roads here are engaging, with a mix of newer asphalt and older, patched sections, and traffic is mostly local and moderate.

From Matera back to Bari, follow secondary highways through rural landscapes, avoiding the busiest Autostrada segments. This creates a satisfying inland loop before the international leg.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Take the ferry from Bari across the Adriatic to Durres in Albania, a common and practical route for motorcyclists. Once disembarked, ride inland to Tirana on national roads that mix urban congestion with open stretches outside the cities.

Albanian roads vary in quality: main routes are generally decent but can have potholes, rough patches, and unpredictable driving behavior from other road users. Keeping a conservative pace and strong situational awareness makes this a realistic and rewarding international finale to a southern Adriatic tour.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Pamplona on secondary mountain roads, quickly trading city traffic for tight, wooded climbs into the foothills of the Pyrenees. The pavement is mostly good but narrower than major highways, with frequent hairpins and short sightlines that reward precise control.

The stretch through the Roncal valley to Isaba is pure motorcycling territory: steep slopes, riverside sections, and a steady mix of second- and third-gear corners. Expect occasional rough patches near drainage and be alert for livestock and local traffic.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Climb toward the Belagua area on a route that becomes higher and more exposed, with sweeping bends and a cooler mountain climate. Pavement is generally good but may show winter wear near the pass, and fog can roll in quickly.

Dropping back toward Ochagavía, the road tightens and dives through forested slopes, alternating fast sweepers with tighter switchbacks. It is a technical but rewarding day, ideal for riders who enjoy linking multiple passes and valleys.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Head northwest on quieter provincial roads through beech forests and rolling hills, a softer but still engaging landscape compared with the high Pyrenean passes. Surfaces vary from very smooth to slightly patched, and some sections can be damp under tree cover.

Approaching San Sebastián, the riding shifts to coastal and urban edges, with more traffic but still enough curves and elevation changes to stay interesting. The finish on the Bay of Biscay is a pleasant contrast to the previous mountain days.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Ride the Basque coast on secondary roads that hug cliffs, dive into small resorts, and occasionally climb inland for broad viewpoints. The pavement is good but the roads can be narrow and busy with local traffic and holidaymakers.

From Zarauz to Bilbao, the character remains varied, with tunnels, short curvy sections, and some more open stretches where you can relax the pace. It’s a compact but full day of mixed coastal and urban riding.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Turn inland on smooth, faster regional roads toward Vitoria-Gasteiz, where broad curves and decent visibility make for efficient touring. Traffic builds near urban centers but quickly thins on linking stretches.

The return to Pamplona traverses rolling farmland and gentle hills, offering a calmer finish with good pavement and predictable geometry. It’s an ideal final day to unwind after more technical mountain sections.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Oviedo on N and regional roads that quickly turn twisty as you approach Cangas de Onís, gateway to the Picos de Europa. The pavement is mostly good, with sustained elevation changes and no shortage of tight bends.

Climbing toward the Covadonga lakes, the road narrows and becomes more exposed, with drop-offs, sharp hairpins, and limited room for error. Expect tourist traffic and livestock; this section rewards smooth throttle and patient overtakes.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Descend back toward Arriondas on the same tight mountain road, then take a more relaxed riverside route toward the coast. The riding blends twistier inland segments with calmer stretches through small towns.

Arriving at Ribadesella, enjoy coastal asphalt with gentle curves and sea views. Pavement is good, but local traffic, pedestrians, and tractors near villages require extra attention.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Follow the Cantabrian coast toward Llanes on secondary roads that weave between cliffs and small beaches. The road isn’t highly technical but has enough bends and elevation changes to stay enjoyable.

Turn inland toward Potes, where the terrain rises sharply into the Picos again. This segment offers some of the best riding in northern Spain: gorge sections, narrow curves, and impressive rock faces close to the road.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Climb toward Fuente Dé on a spectacular valley road, where the asphalt remains good but tightens through short tunnels and carved rock sections. The riding is technical and rewards confident cornering.

From Fuente Dé toward Riaño, the landscape opens into high mountain reservoirs and sweeping curves. Pavement is solid, yet some sections can be exposed to wind and occasional gravel near construction or runoff.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Head south toward León on more open, faster roads, a welcome break after consecutive tight mountain days. The riding is flowing, with good visibility and smoother curves.

Turn northwest back to Oviedo on regional routes that cross gentle hills and rural landscapes, with mostly good pavement and moderate traffic. It’s a balanced, realistic return day that closes the loop without exhaustion.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Málaga heading inland via secondary roads that soon start to climb and twist as you approach the Serranía de Ronda. The pavement is generally good but narrow in places, with sharp curves and frequent elevation changes.

The section into Ronda and on to Setenil is classic southern Spain riding: cliffside views, tight hairpins, and short straights. Expect some tourist traffic near viewpoints but overall an engaging, technical day.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Ride through the white villages on curvy rural roads, with frequent tight bends and short uphill stretches. Pavement varies from very smooth to slightly bumpy, especially near smaller towns.

Approaching Grazalema, the road becomes more mountainous and exposed, with spectacular views and sharper corners cut into the Sierra de Grazalema. This day is demanding but highly rewarding for experienced riders.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Circle through the natural park on twisty, high-quality routes that loop around lakes and limestone cliffs. The curves are continuous, with only short respites, so good rhythm and focus matter.

The descent toward Ubrique uses narrow mountain roads with occasional rockfall and steep drop-offs. Surface grip is generally good but watch for gravel in corners and changing shadows through the day.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Leave the mountains and head toward Jerez on smoother, broader roads that allow a more relaxed pace. Traffic increases near Jerez, but the overall route remains manageable.

Continue to Cádiz with some flatter, coastal sections where the riding is less technical but still pleasant, especially in good weather. Wind from the Atlantic can be strong on exposed parts of the approach.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Head back east on a mix of regional and national roads that cross rolling farmland and low hills. The curves are broader and the traffic moderate, making this a comfortable touring stage.

Approaching Málaga, expect more junctions and urban traffic, but the overall day stays within a realistic distance and effort level. It’s a good, steady finish after several technical mountain stages.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Exit Madrid on secondary routes toward Segovia, quickly leaving multi-lane roads for quieter highways across the plateau. Pavement is good and traffic moderate, with gradual elevation gain.

Climb toward the Navacerrada area on more serpentine mountain roads, where hairpins and short straights give the riding a sporty feel. Weather can be cooler and more changeable at altitude, and weekends can bring heavy local traffic.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Descend on tight mountain roads into forested slopes toward La Granja, with a mix of smooth asphalt and some patched sections from winter wear. Corners come in quick succession, demanding focus.

Continue to Ávila on broader regional roads with long views and rolling terrain. The riding relaxes a bit while still offering enough bends to stay engaging, and the historic city makes a strong overnight stop.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Ride west across Castile on open roads that favor steady cruising rather than tight cornering. Pavement is generally good, but crosswinds on the plateau can be noticeable.

Approaching Ciudad Rodrigo, the landscape becomes slightly more broken and wooded, with a few gentle bends and minor elevation changes. It’s a classic touring day with good progress and big-sky scenery.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Head south into hillier terrain, where the roads start to curve more and pass through pine forests and river valleys. The asphalt is mostly good, with occasional patchwork near smaller towns.

The route to Plasencia includes sections of sweeping bends and some tighter canyon-like segments, giving the day a mix of touring and sport riding characteristics, all on realistic, well-connected roads.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Return toward Madrid via Talavera de la Reina on regional roads that balance open straights with mild curves through farmland and low hills. Traffic increases as you near bigger towns, but the route remains manageable.

The last leg into Madrid uses busier, well-surfaced highways, closing the loop with a practical, realistic approach. It’s a solid end that doesn’t overextend the rider after several varied days.

title: Costa Brava Coastline and Catalan Hills
subtitle: A 5-day tour of Spain

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Barcelona on coastal and nearby secondary roads, avoiding the busiest multilane highways where possible. Once north of the city, the route toward Tossa de Mar becomes noticeably curvier and more scenic.

The section between Tossa and Sant Feliu along the GI-682 is one of the best coastal rides in Spain, with tight bends, cliffs, and short straights. Pavement is good, but the road is narrow and popular, so careful overtaking and a measured pace are essential.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Continue up the Costa Brava on smaller roads that thread between coves, pine forests, and low hills. The riding is a mix of short, tight curves and gentle sweepers, with variable pavement but generally good grip.

The climb toward Begur adds more elevation and cornering, with some narrow village streets and tight switchbacks. It’s a compact but technical day suitable for riders who enjoy coastal-hill combinations.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Ride inland to Figueres on smoother, faster roads, then turn back toward the Cap de Creus peninsula. Traffic is moderate, but visibility is good.

The approach to Cadaqués involves tighter, more exposed coastal hills, with frequent bends and some sections without generous run-off. Wind can be strong, and the combination of curves and sightseeing traffic demands alert riding.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Loop back via Roses on curvy coastal roads, then aim inland toward Girona, where the terrain smooths out into rolling farmland and forest. Pavement is generally good and corners more flowing.

Girona offers an attractive historic center and good services, and the approach is less demanding than earlier coastal segments, giving a more relaxed touring day while still keeping things scenic.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Ride through the Catalan interior via Vic on secondary roads that weave over low ridges and valleys. The curves are moderate, with occasional tighter sections near hills.

Return to Barcelona via well-connected regional roads that gradually increase in traffic but remain realistic for a touring motorcycle. It’s a balanced close to a mixed coastal and inland loop.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Cardiff on the A470 and smaller B-roads into the Brecon Beacons, quickly trading urban traffic for climbing valley roads and open moorland. The route toward Brecon is flowing, with good pavement, steady elevation changes, and wide views across the hills.

Continue west on sweeping A- and B-roads toward Llandovery, taking in classic Welsh bends and occasional narrow, hedged lanes. Surface quality is mostly excellent, though some minor roads can have rough patches and gravel at the edges, rewarding confident cornering and good observation.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Head north on the A483 and then cut across mid-Wales on smaller roads, working through rolling hills, wooded sections, and occasional tighter, blind bends. Traffic is usually light, but sheep and farm vehicles are common, so caution is essential.

Approaching Machynlleth, the road runs close to valley sides and rivers, mixing medium-speed curves with short bursts of open throttle. Pavement can vary from smooth to slightly broken near drainage and bridge joints, adding character without becoming truly rough.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Ride into Snowdonia on the A487 and A470, a superb combination of sweeping corners, long climbs, and descents between steep-sided mountains. Visibility is generally good, but weather can change quickly, with mist and showers affecting grip.

The road to Betws-y-Coed is a well-known motorcycling stretch, with a mix of open, fast curves and tighter sections through forests and stone villages. Surfaces are mostly solid, though some patches near mountain passes can carry loose chippings or damp leaves.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Work deeper into Snowdonia on the A5 and then toward Llanberis, tackling narrower roads that snake between high ridges and lakes. This area delivers tighter bends, short steep ramps, and occasional stone walls close to the road edge, calling for precise positioning.

From Llanberis to Porthmadog the route relaxes slightly, offering sweeping coastal approaches and mixed rural traffic. Expect occasional single-lane sections with passing places and rougher surfaces where the road crosses old bridges and minor passes.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Head south on coastal and inland A-roads to Aberystwyth, taking in broad, undulating routes with medium-speed curves and views across Cardigan Bay. Road quality is generally good, but wind exposure can be significant along the coast.

Turn back toward Cardiff via mid-Wales, mixing faster A-road stretches with some tighter B-road diversions. The final approach becomes busier, yet still offers sections of enjoyable riding before returning to city traffic.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Inverness west on the A862 and A9 before moving onto smaller roads toward Beauly and the west coast. The riding quickly becomes scenic, with gentle curves and loch-side stretches where traffic is modest but can include touring coaches.

Approaching Applecross via the Bealach na Bà pass, the road narrows into single-track with hairpins, steep gradients, and exposed sections. Pavement is decent but can be uneven and gravelly in places, demanding low-speed control and confidence in tight corners.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Follow the coastal single-track north toward Shieldaig and then on to Gairloch, threading along cliff edges, sea inlets, and small villages. This is slow but incredibly rewarding riding, with limited overtaking and frequent blind summits.

The road surface varies from smooth to patchy and can be slippery in wet or misty conditions. Patience and careful throttle control make the day enjoyable, with constant opportunities to stop and take in the Highland scenery.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Ride north via Ullapool on a mixture of A- and B-roads, which offer more open curves and better surfaces than some of the coastal single-track. Traffic is light, with occasional trucks and camper vans.

North of Ullapool toward Lochinver, the road becomes narrower again, with technical bends and sudden changes in radius. It is a superb motorcycling stretch, though it requires strong observation and respect for oncoming traffic.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Turn inland toward Lairg, crossing wild moorland on quiet single- and double-track roads. The surface is generally good, but livestock and deer are common, and wind exposure can be high on the open stretches.

Continue south to Aviemore, reaching the Cairngorm foothills. Roads widen and flow more, with well-engineered bends, good visibility, and a satisfying combination of elevation changes and forest-lined straights.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Ride through Speyside on the A95 and surrounding roads, enjoying broad curves, good tarmac, and a more relaxed rhythm. Traffic includes local cars and occasional lorries but is rarely dense.

The final return to Inverness over the A9 corridor mixes faster sections with tighter bends near passes and bridges. This shorter day wraps the loop with a comfortable, scenic ride rather than a demanding marathon.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Plymouth west on coastal B-roads and the A38, quickly dropping into narrower lanes toward Looe. Expect tight bends, high hedges, and limited visibility, with occasional rough patches and sand on corners near beaches.

Continue toward Falmouth via coastal and inland routes, mixing smoother A-roads with smaller, twistier sections through villages. This day emphasizes technical low-speed control and accurate cornering rather than outright pace.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Ride along the south coast toward Penzance, using a blend of main and minor roads that follow the shoreline and cross short ridges. Surfaces are mostly good, but narrow sections can have gravel and broken edges.

Continue to St Just near Land’s End for rugged Atlantic views and slow, tricky backroads. The riding is often tight and undulating, with blind crests and occasional livestock on the lane, favoring careful, precise handling.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Move up the north coast, where roads become a touch wider but remain full of short, sharp bends and elevation changes. The route around St Ives and toward Newquay has busy tourist traffic, so overtakes must be patient and planned.

Surfaces are generally good, with occasional speed humps and tight village pinch points. The combination of coastal views and rolling inland sections makes this day engaging for riders who enjoy constant input.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Head inland toward Bodmin on the A39/A30 corridor and linked B-roads, transitioning from beach traffic to moorland and wooded landscapes. Roads are smoother and faster, with broader curves and better sightlines.

Approaching Tavistock near Dartmoor, the ride gains elevation and more open views. Side roads onto the moor can be narrow and bumpy, with animals and walkers, so keeping to chosen, sensible routes is wise on a loaded tourer.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Ride across Dartmoor via Princetown, enjoying open moorland roads with sweeping bends, sudden dips, and free-roaming ponies. The surfaces are mostly good but can carry loose gravel and damp patches, particularly near shaded sections.

Drop back toward Plymouth on curving A- and B-roads, with more traffic but still enjoyable riding. The shorter distance lets you savor the moorland sections without fatigue, ending a compact coastal-and-moor loop.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Lancaster north toward Kendal on the A6 and linked roads, gradually entering hillier terrain. Surfaces are generally solid, with mild curves and medium traffic levels.

From Kendal, head into the Lake District on the A591, where the bends tighten and gradients increase. The approach to Keswick offers a mix of sweeping corners and narrower lakeside sections, sometimes crowded with holiday traffic but very rewarding for experienced riders.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Tackle Honister Pass and nearby single-track roads, with steep ramps, tight hairpins, and rougher tarmac in spots. These high passes demand low-speed control, good braking, and caution on wet or gravel-strewn surfaces.

Drop south toward Ambleside, following narrow lakeside roads where visibility is limited by stone walls and foliage. Traffic can be heavy at peak times, turning the day into a technical and concentration-heavy ride.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Exit the Lakes via Windermere and head into the Yorkshire Dales, picking up roads like the A684 with flowing bends and rolling scenery. Pavement is generally good, with some broken edges on minor lanes.

Around Hawes and Reeth the riding becomes a classic dales experience: tight stone-walled lanes, blind summits, and sudden dips. Good road positioning and moderate speeds make this day enjoyable rather than stressful.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Ride east and then loop back north-west across rural northern England on mixed A- and B-roads, crossing moors and river valleys. Corners vary from long sweepers to sharp unexpected bends, often signposted but still worth respecting.

Approaching Penrith, roads become slightly busier but stay rewarding, with good surfaces and rolling hills. The route is less extreme than the high passes but retains a strong touring character.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Finish the loop with a run through Shap and back toward Lancaster on rural A-roads paralleling the motorway. These roads are smoother and faster, with open views and predictable bends.

Traffic includes trucks and local traffic, but there are enough quieter stretches to enjoy the bike. It is a relaxed closing day after more technical riding earlier in the route.

title: Northern Ireland Coastal and Sperrin Loop
subtitle: A 5-day tour of United Kingdom

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Belfast north toward Larne on the A8 before joining the Antrim Coast Road, one of the most scenic coastal stretches in the UK. The route hugs cliffs and bays, with medium-speed curves and generally good pavement.

Approaching Cushendun, the road tightens and passes through small villages where surfaces may be patched and narrow. Wind exposure can be significant, and loose gravel occasionally appears at the edges near lay-bys and viewpoints.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Continue along the Causeway Coast, enjoying sweeping bends, short climbs, and descents with open sea views. Traffic is moderate, especially near major attractions like the Giant’s Causeway, so overtakes must be planned.

Road surfaces are generally smooth, though occasional tourist buses and parked cars can make some sections tight. This is a day to savor the view and ride with a smooth, unhurried style.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Head west via Coleraine toward Derry/Londonderry, mixing coastal and inland stretches. The roads transition to more conventional A-roads with broader curves and better overtaking opportunities.

Traffic increases near towns, but surfaces remain good. The day is less technical than the pure coastal riding but offers a balance of touring efficiency and scenery.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Ride through the Sperrin Mountains region on a mix of A- and B-roads that curve over low passes and through valleys. Surfaces vary a little, with occasional rough patches on smaller routes but generally good grip.

Traffic is light, and the riding can be brisk, with open sweeping bends and clear views. This is a good day for steady, confident cornering and enjoying rural Northern Ireland.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Finish by looping south-east through Armagh and back to Belfast, using well-maintained regional roads. Bends are moderate, and traffic volume increases near the cities, but the ride remains comfortable for touring.

This closing stage emphasizes relaxed progress and efficient navigation, tying together coastal and inland sectors into a coherent Northern Ireland loop.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave London via south-east arterial roads, quickly trading city congestion for the rolling lanes of the Kent Downs. Roads near Sevenoaks combine smooth surfaces with medium-speed bends and woodland sections that can be damp in shade.

Continue toward Canterbury on a mix of A-roads and quieter B-roads, avoiding major motorways where possible. Expect occasional narrow lanes with tight hedges and farm traffic, demanding good observation.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Ride to Dover on the A2 and linked roads, a short but busy stretch with steady traffic and good surfaces. The approach includes some faster sections and roundabouts, so lane discipline matters.

Take the ferry or tunnel to Calais for the international crossing, then ride down the French coast to Boulogne-sur-Mer. The French roads are generally smooth and lightly curved, with some coastal wind exposure and moderate holiday traffic.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Follow inland French routes toward Abbeville and Rouen, staying off autoroutes where possible and favoring D-roads with gentle curves and village passages. Surfaces are typically excellent, though some rural sections can have agricultural debris.

The day is more transit-oriented but remains pleasant for motorcyclists thanks to rolling countryside and a steady mix of open stretches and slower village sections. Traffic builds near Rouen, with multi-lane junctions requiring clear navigation.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Head south-west through Normandy on secondary highways, crossing rivers and forested areas. Curves are generally gentle, and the road alignment is relaxed, giving a chance to cruise at a comfortable touring pace.

Villages add periodic slowing points with cobbles, speed bumps, and tight junctions. Overall, surfaces remain good, and traffic is moderate, making it a balanced day in the saddle.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Ride south toward the Loire valley, mixing wider regional roads with occasional smaller detours through farmland and minor ridges. Pavement quality is high, and curves are flowing rather than sharp.

Approaching Tours, traffic increases, but the riding stays manageable. It is a fitting end point in France, with a clear sense of distance covered from London via Kent and Normandy on realistic, scenic roads.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Edinburgh south on the A7 and linked B-roads into the Scottish Borders, enjoying rolling hills, riverside sections, and good-quality tarmac. The bends are mostly medium-speed, with some tighter sequences through woodland.

Continue east toward Berwick-upon-Tweed on scenic roads with light traffic, crossing undulating farmland and small towns. The day balances enjoyable cornering with a calm touring pace.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Ride south along the Northumberland coast and then turn inland toward Newcastle using a mix of coastal A-roads and quieter inland sections. Surfaces are good, but wind and occasional sand on the road near beaches are possible.

Head further south to Durham, where traffic increases and junctions become more complex. The day is less technical and serves as a realistic transitional leg south.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Travel through eastern England on a combination of A-roads that avoid the busiest motorways. The terrain is flatter and more open, with long straights and wide, gentle bends.

Approaching York and Lincoln, expect more traffic and roundabouts, but road surfaces are generally excellent. It is a distance-focused day that remains comfortable on a touring motorcycle.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Ride south across the Fens and into Cambridgeshire, using rural A-roads and occasional B-road connectors. The riding is straightforward, with mostly straight alignments and minimal elevation change.

Closer to London, congestion builds, and lane discipline becomes important. The day shifts from rural touring to careful urban navigation without excessive distance.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Leave London southeast toward Folkestone, choosing A-roads parallel to the motorway where possible to keep the ride more engaging. Traffic can be heavy, but surfaces are strong and bends remain gentle.

Cross the Channel via the Tunnel to Calais for the international leg. Post-crossing riding is short and simple, with smooth French roads and minimal technical challenge, marking a practical cross-border finish.

title: Devon and Dorset to Brittany Shores
subtitle: A 5-day tour of United Kingdom

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Exeter east on the A30 and smaller roads, quickly entering rolling countryside and modest hills. Surfaces are mostly good, with some narrower sections that can feel tight when traffic is heavy.

Approach Lyme Regis via twisting coastal B-roads, with steep ramps, hairpin-like bends, and occasional rough patches near drainage. Good low-speed control and awareness of tourists are essential.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Ride along the Jurassic Coast area toward Dorchester and Weymouth, following B- and A-roads that undulate with the chalk ridges and coastal line. Corners vary from long sweepers to sharp, unsighted bends.

Road surfaces are generally solid, but some village approaches have speed humps and rough patches. The day is compact but packed with varied cornering and scenic sections.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Head east along the south coast, mixing faster A-roads with occasional diversions through seaside towns. Traffic can be busy, particularly near Bournemouth and Poole, but the roads remain suitable for steady touring.

Approaching Portsmouth, navigation becomes more complex with roundabouts and multi-lane segments, yet surfaces are good and lines of sight are generally clear. The day serves as a coastal transit leg toward the cross-Channel port.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Cross from Portsmouth to Caen by ferry, the realistic route for a bike in this sector. After disembarkation, ride through Normandy on D-roads with gentle curves, passing fields, small woods, and historic towns.

Road surfaces are smooth, and traffic is moderate, making it an easy day for covering ground with periodic stops. The run to Bayeux remains scenic without being technically demanding.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Continue west across Normandy into Brittany, staying off toll autoroutes and choosing well-surfaced regional roads. Curves are mostly medium-speed, with occasional tighter village entries.

Approaching Saint-Malo, the route becomes coastal again, with wind exposure and more tourist traffic. It is a satisfying end point, showing a clear progression from Devon lanes to French maritime roads on a realistic touring path.

title: North Wales to Irish Republic Circuit
subtitle: A 5-day tour of United Kingdom

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Leave Liverpool on A-roads toward Chester, quickly moving from urban traffic to more open countryside. Surfaces are generally good, with gentle curves and moderate traffic.

Head into North Wales toward Llangollen on more undulating routes that begin to show tighter bends and small climbs. The riding is engaging but not yet demanding, making it a good introductory day.

days.title: Day 2
days.description:
Ride into the heart of North Wales, using the A5 and related roads that cut through valleys and over low passes. Corners tighten and elevation changes become more pronounced, with generally solid tarmac but occasional rough patches.

Approach Bangor via scenic routes with mixed traffic, including camper vans and coaches. The day is a satisfying blend of technical and flowing riding through classic Welsh scenery.

days.title: Day 3
days.description:
Ride to Holyhead for the ferry crossing to Dublin, following the A55 corridor with smooth, faster curves and good surfaces. Wind exposure on bridges and coastal sections can be strong.

After disembarking in Dublin, traffic density increases significantly, but roads are well marked and surfaced. The day mixes touring into Holyhead with urban navigation at the destination.

days.title: Day 4
days.description:
Leave Dublin south into County Wicklow, quickly stepping onto narrower, twistier roads in the Wicklow Mountains. Elevation changes and tight bends make this a more technical riding day.

Around Glendalough, roads can be single-lane with rough edges, damp patches, and occasional loose gravel. Careful throttle and braking control are rewarded with superb views and engaging riding.

days.title: Day 5
days.description:
Ride south-west through rural Ireland on regional roads, enjoying a mix of medium-speed bends, rolling hills, and small villages. Surfaces are generally good, though some sections can be bumpy with patched repairs.

Finish in Waterford after a relaxed but varied day, suitable for a touring motorcycle with luggage. The route provides a realistic cross-border journey from North Wales into the Republic of Ireland, balancing technical mountain sections with smoother valley riding.

title: Lake Garda to Dolomite Legends Route locations: Day 1: Sirmione, Lake Garda (45.4920, 10.6070) Tremosine sul Garda, Strada della Forra (45.7685, 10.7557) Riva del Garda (45.8869, 10.8405) Day 1 distance: 130 km Description: Start on the southern shore of Lake Garda at Sirmione, then work your way up the western side using lakeside secondary roads instead of the main highway. The riding quickly becomes engaging, with medium-speed curves, short tunnels, and occasional tight sections where the road hangs above the water. Traffic can be busy in summer, but the pavement is generally excellent and the views are constant.
subtitle: A 2-day tour of Italy

days.title: Day 1
days.description: Leave Riva del Garda on mountain roads heading northeast into Trentino, trading the lakeside for forested climbs and wider valley routes. The road surface is mostly smooth, with long sequences of linked bends and steady elevation gain. Traffic is moderate, mainly local cars and touring bikes, and there are frequent chances to enjoy sweeping corners at a comfortable pace.Approach Cavalese and then Canazei via well-built alpine roads with properly cambered turns and good visibility. As you near Canazei, gradients steepen and hairpins become more frequent, but the tarmac remains strong. This is classic Dolomite riding: constant curves, high cliffs around you, and frequent opportunities to stop for viewpoints without breaking the flow of the ride.

days.title: Day 2
days.description: From Canazei, climb directly to Passo Pordoi, tackling a dense series of hairpins on a well-surfaced high-mountain pass. The gradients are steep but predictable, and the road is engineered for good cornering lines, though you must watch for buses, cyclists, and loose gravel near the apexes. The descent brings similar technical turns, rewarding precise braking and smooth throttle work.Loop across Passo Sella, where the road narrows in places and clings to the mountainside with exposed sections and changing radii in the bends. Continue toward Passo Giau, one of Italy’s most iconic passes, combining tight uphill switchbacks, fast open sections, and panoramic views. The final drop into Cortina d’Ampezzo blends flowing curves with busier valley traffic, closing a compact three-day, roughly 350 km route that strings together Lake Garda, Strada della Forra, and the standout Dolomite passes into one concentrated mountain-touring experience.

days.title: Day 1
days.description:
Start on the southern shore of Lake Garda at Sirmione, then work your way up the western side using lakeside secondary roads instead of the main highway. The riding quickly becomes engaging, with medium-speed curves, short tunnels, and occasional tight sections where the road hangs above the water. Traffic can be busy in summer, but the pavement is generally excellent and the views are constant.

Climb toward Tremosine and the Strada della Forra, a legendary narrow gorge road carved into the cliff. Here you’ll find tight hairpins, single-lane sections, rock overhangs, and variable grip, demanding low-speed precision and good clutch control. Continue north to Riva del Garda on flowing lakeside stretches that allow a relaxed end to a technical, scenic day.
